number_of_offences: Charges were framed under Sections 7 and 13(1)(d) read with Section 13(2) of the PC Act, but the number of offences/counts charged and upheld is not stated
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the evidence that the second respondent, Ravi Bhatt, was privy to the offence and that his statement under Section 164 Cr.P.C. was crucial to prove the missing links in the circumstantial evidence.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses, including the second respondent, as credible in the context of the investigation and trial, noting that his statement was examined and cross-examined.
trial_duration: The trial proceeded in the Court of Special Judge, evidence was concluded as against the Appellant on 24.7.2008, and the Appellant was convicted by the Special Judge vide his judgment dated 24.5.2010.
legal_representation: Shri P.C. Mishra appeared in person; Shri Rajiv Nanda, C.K. Sharma, B.V. Balaram Das, V. Mohana for the Respondents.
investigation_status: The CBI registered R.C. No.1 S(A) 96 DLI dated 29.2.1996 under Section 7 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988. The investigation culminated with the recording of the statement of the second Respondent under Section 164 Cr.P.C. on 7.8.1996. The CBI filed an application under Section 306 Cr.P.C. before the Special Judge on 24.10.1996 for grant of pardon to the second Respondent, which was passed by the Metropolitan Magistrate on 2.11.1996.
procedural_irregularity: The Metropolitan Magistrate granted pardon to the second Respondent during investigation, which was considered a curable irregularity under Section 460(g) Cr.P.C. provided the order was passed in good faith.
appeal_history: The Appellant filed an application under the proviso to Section 234 Cr.P.C. before the Special Judge on 24.7.2008, which was rejected. The High Court dismissed the appellant's revision petition. The appeal was dismissed by the Supreme Court.
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the Metropolitan Magistrate had the power to grant pardon during investigation under Section 306 Cr.P.C. and that the order was passed in good faith, making it a curable irregularity under Section 460(g) Cr.P.C.
defence_argument: The accused argued that the Metropolitan Magistrate did not have the power to grant pardon as the matter was already under the jurisdiction of the Special Judge under the PC Act, and the order was without jurisdiction.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that during investigation, both the Special Judge and the Magistrate acting under Section 306 Cr.P.C. have concurrent jurisdiction to grant pardon, and that an order passed in good faith is a curable irregularity.
precedent_relied_upon: Kanta Prashad v. Delhi Administration 1958 SCR 1218, State of U.P. v. Kai/ash Nath Agarwal and others 1973 (3) SCR 728, A. Devendran v. State of Tamil Nadu 1997 (4) Suppl. SCR 591, AR. Antulay v. Ramdas Sriniwas Nayak and another 1984 (2) SCR 914, Dilawar Singh v. Parvinder Singh alias Iqbal Singh and another 2005 (5) Suppl. SCR 83, Harshad S. Mehta and others v. State of Maharashtra 2001 (2) Suppl. SCR 577, Bangaru Laxman v. State (through CBI) and another 2011 (13) SCR 268
